title: Visiting
goal: Visit a Slovak home without putting a foot wrong, turn down second helpings without giving offense, and close this book with something no grammar table covers: manners.
bekal: behave correctly from the front door to saying goodbye
decline and accept offers of food with the right phrases
switch from *vy* to *ty* at the right moment — and know who gets to offer it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — U Evy doma
dialogs.intro: Eva has invited Budi to dinner at her parents' home in Košice. Her mother opens the door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dobrý večer. Toto je pre vás.
lines.id: Good evening. This is for you.

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.text: Ó, kvety! To ste nemuseli. Ďakujem pekne.

notes: **Poďte ďalej** literally "come further" — the standard phrase for inviting someone in. The informal form is *poď ďalej*. There's no literal "come in" in Slovak; you're invited to come **forward**, not in.

**To ste nemuseli** literally "you didn't have to" — the standard reply when receiving a gift. It's not a refusal; it's an acknowledgment that the gift goes beyond what was expected. Just smile in return, or say *maličkosť* ("it's nothing much").

**Môžeš mu tykať** — Eva lets her mother switch to *ty*. Notice who offers it: **the older person, or the one of higher status**. As a young guest, Budi must not offer it first. The verbs are *tykať* (to say *ty*) and *vykať* (to say *vy*) — two verbs made from the pronouns themselves.

**Mám si vyzuť topánky?** is a question you should ask once; in Slovakia the answer is almost always yes. Taking your shoes off in someone's home is an unspoken rule, and hosts usually keep *papuče* (house slippers) for their guests.
**Ďakujem, navzájom** is the standard reply to *dobrú chuť*. The word *navzájom* means "mutually", and it's also used to return any kind of good wishes: *Šťastný nový rok!* — *Navzájom!*

grammars.title: Tykať and vykať — and who decides
body: Switching from *vy* to *ty* is a real social event in Slovakia, not just a grammar choice. There are rules, and they aren't written down anywhere except on pages like this one.

head: Situation
Form
Note
rows: people your age, new acquaintances at a party

after: **The one who offers is always the older person or the one of higher status.** The phrase: *Môžeme si tykať?* The answer: *Áno, samozrejme* or *Rád / rada*. After that there's no going back — switching back to *vy* would read as a rift in the relationship.

**If you're not sure, use *vy* and wait.** That's not excessive caution; it's what Slovaks do themselves. Using *ty* too soon with an older person is one of the few language mistakes that genuinely comes across as rude.

**A useful exception:** among young people, online, and between fellow hikers, *ty* is used almost at once. On mountain trails, even strangers greet each other with *ahoj* — a habit that survives from the old hiking clubs.

grammars.title: Accepting and declining
body: A Slovak host will offer more at least twice, and the first refusal is often taken as mere politeness. That's why a refusal that works needs a particular structure.

head: Sentence
What it really means
When to use it
rows: I really can't eat any more.

after: **Don't use *nechcem* (I don't want) to turn down food.** It sounds like you're rejecting the cooking, not the amount. *Nemôžem* moves the reason to your stomach, not to the food — and that difference is felt.
**Praise is required, not optional.** *Bolo to výborné* or *veľmi mi chutilo* is part of the refusal, not separate small talk. Declining without praising is the part foreign guests most often miss.

**If you have dietary restrictions, say so early, not at the table.** *Nejem bravčové mäso* or *Jem len halal* is said when you're invited, by message, a few days ahead. A Slovak host will adjust the whole menu without complaint — but only if they know before they start cooking.

blocks.text: **Bryndza** is a soft sheep's cheese at the heart of Slovak cooking, salty and sharp. Many foreigners don't like it at first bite; almost all change their minds by the third try. If you want one dish that explains the country, *bryndzové halušky* is the answer.

blocks.title: Toasting
items: *Na zdravie!* — "To health!" The same phrase is used when someone sneezes.

The rule to follow: **look each other in the eye** as the glasses clink, one by one, all around the table. Looking at the glass instead of the eyes is considered impolite, and in some families it's said to bring bad luck.
*Slivovica* is usually poured before the meal, not after — and you can decline with *ďakujem, nepijem alkohol*. This refusal is fully respected and needs no explanation.

blocks.title: Three small things people notice
items: **Flowers in odd numbers.** Even-numbered bunches are for funerals. Three, five, or seven stems — not four or six.
**Arrive on time, not early.** Five minutes late is safe; ten minutes early makes the host panic.
**Offer to help clear the table.** Your offer will almost certainly be turned down, but making it gets noticed — and not making it gets noticed too.

sections.title: Twenty units, and what comes next

blocks.text: If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, it's worth looking back for a moment. You started this book without a single word, and now you can introduce yourself, ask for directions, order food, shop in the right quantities, say you're ill, talk about last weekend, make plans for next week, and visit someone's home without putting a foot wrong.

More importantly: you've used **all six cases** of Slovak, each for a clear everyday job, not as a table to memorize. And you've made it through **perfective and imperfective verb pairs** — the part with no real equivalent in English, and the one that makes many people give up in the second month.

blocks.title: Three things that will move you forward fastest now
items: **Speak before you're ready.** Slovaks rarely meet foreigners who want to learn their language, and even the smallest effort is welcomed with a warmth that may surprise you. A wrong sentence spoken teaches more than a correct sentence only read.
**Note nouns with their gender, and verbs with their partner.** This ten-second habit is what separates people who keep progressing from people who get stuck at A2.
**Listen to something every day, even if you don't understand it yet.** Your ear is built by time, not talent. Radio, songs, children's news — anything, as long as it's every day.
